HEATING OIL: Prices are back above the spring peak as winter starts, and suppliers are to be regulated for the first time

Homes that heat with oil, which means much of rural Carmarthenshire, Gower, the valleys and Pembrokeshire, are to get a regulator for the first time.

The UK Government said on Tuesday it will accept the Competition and Markets Authority’s call for rules covering heating oil suppliers, after a spring in which the price in Wales rose from 64p a litre in February to 106p in March.

That is a rise of two thirds in a month, by the CMA’s figures. Prices eased over the summer, but comparison sites put the UK average back above 120p a litre with VAT by mid-September, and it was around 121p on Tuesday.

Around 100,000 Welsh households, 7% of the total, rely on heating oil, according to Senedd researchers. Unlike gas and electricity it has no price cap, no regulator and no ombudsman.

Orders cancelled, then re-sold at the higher price

The spike followed the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East. Some suppliers cancelled orders already placed, then sold the oil again at the new price, the CMA found.

The CMA found around 1,700 customers caught that way, and estimated they paid £150 to £350 more for replacement oil than they had agreed.

Those suppliers have now agreed to pay up, the CMA said in August. Customers who bought replacement oil get the difference refunded, and those who did not get their original order at the original price.

Around 800 customers had been contacted by then, and the CMA says the rest will be. Nobody needs to apply, but anyone claiming for a replacement order should keep the receipt and delivery note.

Sarah Cardell, the CMA’s chief executive, said: “Heating oil isn’t a luxury, it’s a necessity that many people rely on to have hot water and warm homes.”

What the new rules would cover, and the 500-litre minimum

Across Britain a typical 500-litre order went from about £320 in February to about £520 in March, the CMA said.

The CMA’s market study in July found the market generally competitive, with the price rise driven mostly by wholesale costs, and no evidence suppliers made unusual profits from the crisis.

Its recommendation, now accepted, is for suppliers to register and meet minimum standards on quoting prices, handling cancellations and giving customers access to independent dispute resolution.

Ministers say they will work with the industry on the regime, and in the meantime the voluntary codes of conduct suppliers sign up to will be strengthened. No date has been given for the rules.

The practice of setting a minimum order of 500 litres, which forces some households to buy more than they need in one go, is to be reviewed.

Domestic tanks typically hold 1,000 to 2,000 litres, so a 500-litre minimum is a quarter to half a tank at a time.

Polly Billington, the Minister for Energy Consumers, said thousands of customers “felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year”.

She added: “We won’t accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they’re protected in the market.”

No price cap, and prices still close to double last year’s

What the plan does not do is cap the price. The charity National Energy Action has called for the Ofgem price cap to be extended to heating oil, and there is no sign of the government proposing that.

Prices remain close to double what they were a year ago, and one customer told the BBC this week he had been quoted 111p a litre.

The latest climb is driven by the same thing as the spring one. Tankers are still barely getting through the Strait of Hormuz, global stocks are down by more than 500 million barrels since February according to the International Energy Agency, and refiners are prioritising diesel, fuel distributors say.

Tim Buckman, chief executive of the comparison site BoilerJuice, told the BBC that regulation on its own “is not going to reduce the price for customers”, and that taking VAT off heating oil would.

£53m of help, and the £9,000 to get off oil altogether

The government put £53m into emergency help for low-income heating oil customers during the spike, paid out through councils, which set their own rules on who qualifies. Wales’s share was announced in March as £3.8m, at a time when rural homes were also being warned about thieves draining tanks.

In Wales that became a £200 payment for households on the Council Tax Reduction Scheme who heat with oil or LPG, and a higher Discretionary Assistance Fund limit of £750 for others in hardship, according to a Senedd Research briefing in May. The Welsh Government‘s Nest service gives free energy advice.

Households on oil can also claim £9,000 off a heat pump under the Boiler Upgrade Scheme, a grant raised from £7,500 in July and available until March next year.

Applications hit a record 8,150 in July, up 81% on June, according to the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. In August, 1,042 of the grants paid out were the £9,000 oil-to-heat-pump rate, a third of the month’s total.

One of them went to Anne, who replaced the oil boiler in her off-grid Victorian cottage in Wales. “When the price of oil suddenly doubled, I thought, ‘Well, this is just bonkers,'” she said.

The CMA also recommended a register of vulnerable households so suppliers know who to prioritise when deliveries are short.

PETROL PRICES: Google Maps now shows you the cheapest fuel near you

Drivers can now see what every forecourt around them is charging before they set off, with near real-time petrol and diesel prices appearing on Google Maps in the UK from today.

Search “petrol” in the app and each station’s unleaded price appears on its pin. Tap through and the station page breaks it down by fuel, including super unleaded and premium diesel.

The prices come from Fuel Finder, the UK Government scheme under which every petrol station has had to report a price change within 30 minutes since February, or risk a fine.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero says around 99% of all fuel sold on UK roads is now covered, and that a household with a car could save about £40 a year by shopping around.

How it works

Fuel prices on Google Maps pins; the government’s screenshots are from Manchester (Image: DESNZ / Google) A station page showing prices by fuel type (Image: DESNZ / Google)

Fuel Finder was set up on the recommendation of the Competition and Markets Authority, which can act against stations where there is evidence they are not reporting.

The data already sits behind the price displays in Waze, the PetrolPrices app, the AA, Confused.com and RAC Fuel Watch. Google Maps puts it in front of the millions who never open a dedicated fuel app.

Polly Billington, the Minister for Energy Consumers, said: “Tackling the affordability crisis is our first responsibility and for so many families and businesses, petrol and diesel are essential goods, not luxuries.”

“Accessing the cheapest fuel should be simple, which is why it is a game-changer for near real-time fuel prices to be shown on Google Maps for the first time in the UK, helping drivers find the best deal and save money at the pump.”

Sarah-Jayne Williams, Google’s director of global product partnerships for Geo, said: “Integrating Fuel Finder data into Google Maps and Waze gives drivers visibility on nearby pump prices, helping drivers make intentional choices to help their budgets go further this winter.”

Why it matters this autumn

Pump prices have been high since the Iran war began in February. In May petrol hit 158.52p a litre, its highest since the conflict started, and Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, froze fuel duty until the end of the year.

On Wednesday afternoon several Swansea forecourts were charging 173p a litre for unleaded and 199p for diesel. The petrol price is around 15p above the 158.52p that counted as a high in May.

That 5p duty cut, first made in 2022, runs until at least 31 December. What happens to it after that has not been announced.

The government says the Maps launch is the latest of its cost of living measures, pointing to the VAT cut on electricity bills and the £2 cap on bus fares.

Because the data is near real-time, a station that cuts its price after lunch should show the new figure within the half hour. One that does not report risks a CMA fine.

The government describes the Middle East conflict as the reason prices have been pushed up; by May the RAC Foundation had put drivers’ “war premium” at £3bn.

ENERGY BILLS: VAT scrapped from electricity – but you’ll still pay more

The 5% VAT on household electricity has gone. It came off at midnight, standing charge and prepayment top-ups included, and there is nothing to claim.

Ofgem‘s new price cap kicked in at the same moment, up 4%. A typical home using gas and electricity now pays £1,723 a year, £60 more than over the summer, about £5 a month.

Without the tax cut that rise would have been around £45 bigger. So for most homes the bill has still gone up, just by less than it would have.

The £45 is a Britain-wide figure. The average South Wales electricity bill was £1,129 in 2024, among the highest in Britain, and 5% of that is around £56, so a typical home here keeps a little more than the headline number.

Gas keeps its VAT

Gas is doing the driving, up about 8% under the new cap, and gas keeps its 5% VAT. Homes heated by electricity alone see a rise of under 1% and keep the most from the cut.

Heating oil keeps its 5% VAT too, and sits outside the price cap altogether, so the thousands of oil-heated homes across rural Carmarthenshire and Gower get the cut on their electricity and nothing on the tank. The £9,000 heat pump grant for swapping an oil boiler, raised by £1,500 in July as oil prices climbed, is the government’s offer on that side.

The cut runs to the end of March. The government says it is funded for this financial year and has not said what happens after that.

Around a third of households are on a fixed deal and never see the price cap. The government’s own guidance says the VAT cut applies to fixed tariffs too, and ministers say they “expect” suppliers to pass it on, which would mean a fall for those customers.

“The one they dread the most”

“For many families, the energy bill is the one they dread the most,” said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. “I don’t accept that it has to be this way, and I am determined to bring down costs for good. But I know people can’t wait. Families need breathing space now.”

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the cut “will give households some much needed breathing space”, on top of “the £150 of costs we removed from bills earlier this year”.

Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the government was “working to reindustrialise Wales”, naming floating offshore wind, small modular reactors and compound semiconductors, and that “as we approach the winter we are also making sure that people across Wales will have more room to breathe”.

The fixes that stop at the border

The tax cut applies across the UK. Several of the other “everyday fixes” the Prime Minister listed alongside it do not. The £2 bus fare cap from January is for England; transport is devolved, and Wales has £1 fares for under-22s and no cap for most adults.

Business rates are devolved too. Wales’s own cut, 30% for pubs, cafés, restaurants and gyms with a rateable value under £51,000, starts in April 2027.

What does cross the border is the £150 Warm Home Discount, which the government says will reach around six million households this winter, and the £150 taken off bills at last year’s Budget.

Who gets the £150

The discount is not paid out; your electricity supplier takes it off the bill. You qualify if, on 23 August, you or your partner were on Universal Credit, Housing Benefit, income-related ESA or Pension Credit, your supplier is in the scheme, and one of your names is on the electricity bill. The scheme reopens this month.

Last month Age Cymru said more than half the older people it surveyed were already rationing their heating, and asked for the discount to go to £200 with a route to apply for people not on those benefits. It stays at £150, and there is no application route.

Four in ten people struggling with bills never ask for help, with embarrassment the biggest reason. Anyone struggling can contact their supplier, which must offer support.

What comes next

Earlier this week the Prime Minister announced Great British Grid, a new publicly owned body inside Great British Energy, which he says will bring energy costs into line with the rest of Europe within ten years.

Ofgem’s next price cap announcement is on 25 November and covers January to March, the coldest quarter and the last three months of the VAT cut.

ALCOHOL: Cheapest booze goes up 30% in Wales from today, and the deaths it was meant to stop are at a record

The floor price of alcohol in Wales goes up by nearly a third from Thursday, and the strongest cheap drinks on the shelf will feel it most.

From 1 October nothing can be sold for less than 65p a unit, up from the 50p that has applied since March 2020. A three-litre bottle of white cider, around 22 units, cannot now be sold for less than about £14.30. A bottle of wine starts at £5.85, a litre of vodka at £24.38, a four-pack of strong lager at £5.20.

It is not a tax. The extra money stays with the shop and the producer, not the Welsh Government.

“Someone’s parent, partner or child”

Ministers say the change could prevent more than 900 alcohol-related deaths and help nearly 5,000 people cut down on harmful drinking over the next 20 years.

“Every one of the hundreds of lives this change could save is someone’s parent, partner or child,” said Nerys Evans, the deputy minister for public and preventative health. “That’s why this matters.”

The 50p rate, she said, “has been made less effective by inflation”, worth 39p in 2020 money, “so raising it to 65p is not about punishing people who drink responsibly, it’s about closing that gap”.

Andrew Misell of Alcohol Change UK said the new price “will keep big bottles of super-strength cider off the shelves” and make bulk discounts harder, “and all this without pushing up the price of a pint in pubs”.

Deaths at a record while the 50p price was in force

Alcohol-specific deaths in Wales reached a record 562 in 2023, or 17.7 per 100,000 people. That is higher than before minimum pricing came in.

When the rise was put out to consultation last summer, the Welsh Conservatives called the policy a failure, pointing to a 50% rise in alcohol-related deaths between 2019 and 2023, and Darren Millar said it should be scrapped in favour of “the inadequate investment in addiction services”.

The government’s answer is that the pandemic and the cost of living crisis got in the way, and that the policy has still been “broadly positive”.

Skipped meals and a switch to spirits

Five years at 50p cleared the cheap high-strength drinks from the shelves and consumption appears to have fallen. Some dependent drinkers skipped meals or bills to keep drinking, and others switched from cider to spirits.

Iola Ynyr, a writer from Gwynedd who has spoken about her own alcoholism, told the BBC last year that price does not change a dependent drinker. “If someone’s addicted, they’ll find a way to get alcohol. It’s the families who suffer.”

The academics who reviewed the policy wanted it kept, the price raised, and treatment funded properly. The Welsh Government says it spends more than £68m a year on people affected by alcohol and drugs, £41m of it on local services.

Wales now charges the same as Scotland, which went to 65p in 2024. England has no minimum price, so the drive over the bridge for a boot full of cider is the one effect everyone expected and, so far, nobody has found.

That Damn Debt

The official U.S. total public debt outstanding breached $40 trillion for the first time in history. It stands at $40,047,426,000,000 according to data released by the U.S. Department of the Treasury. It has increased by about three trillion dollars since January 20, 2025, when the current administration took office.

Considering how much he likes to brag about setting records you’d think Donnie Trump would be in front of the cameras proclaiming, “Biggest debt in history! No one has ever seen a debt as big as this. America is first! We’re winning.”

Instead, fearless leader is attending auto races and showing off his new helipad, $5 million dollars’ worth of big, ugly, granite adorned with his name and sitting on the White House lawn. Something else a future president will have to remove.

Trump left it to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to downplay the event, blame the record debt on Joe Biden, and insist the economy will “grow” out of it. The problem with that is obvious. The economy is growing at a rate of about 2%. The debt is growing at the rate of about 6%. As they say, the math ain’t mathin’.

To be fair, as the graph above makes clear, the debt has been growing steadily for decades under both Republican and Democratic administrations. Some of that is growth. Some of that is inflation. The key to watch is not the total debt amount but the ratio of debt to the nation’s total economic output, the GDP. The debt-to-GDP ratio compares a country’s total government debt to its gross domestic product (GDP). It shows a country’s ability to pay back its debts. The U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio is now roughly 124% to 125%.

Trump has stated dozens of times across his campaigns and presidencies that he would control, reduce, or completely eliminate the national debt and federal deficit, famously vowing during his 2016 campaign to wipe out the entire national debt within eight years. Despite these promises, Trump legislative actions, such as the 2017 and 2025 tax cuts, caused substantial increases in annual budget deficits and the overall national debt.

As this graph shows, there is a pattern which began in the Reagan years. The Republicans cut taxes without cutting spending. That increases the annual budget deficit and accelerates increases in the debt. Democrats take control and reduce the deficit, only to have the Republicans repeat the trend the next time they get in control. (By the way, I had AI assistance in doing the actual drawing, but I am responsible for finding the numbers and designing both graphs. The numbers come from the Federal Reserve and the Department of Commerce.).

While Republicans like to blame Democrats for the debt, the facts don’t bear that out.

This graphic summarizes the changes in the total debt going all the way back to the Reagan administration. It was then that I first heard the term “trickle-down economics.” The idea was that if you cut taxes for the top backets, they will spend more money, and the effects will pass down to the people in lower brackets. It sounded good to me at the time. But the evidence since has shown it doesn’t work. Nothing trickles. The rich just get richer and the gap between the rich and the rest of us grows larger.

To finance the debt the government borrows money., It does that by issuing securities, Treasury Notes and Bonds. The interest rate it pays is the “cost” of borrowing. More borrowing, more securities. To convince investors to keep buying trillions of dollars in new debt, the U.S. government must offer competitive interest rates. The 10-year treasury yield is currently about 4.7%. The bond market is struggling to meet the demand.

Bessent is doubling long-term government bond buybacks to curb rising rates and inject liquidity into the debt market. On August 19, 2026, the Treasury Department shocked Wall Street by announcing it will increase its buyback operations for 10-year to 30-year bonds to at least $4 billion per operation, up from the previous $2 billion cap. Bessent is executing a strategy he calls a “Treasury Twist“. By purchasing less-liquid, older (“off-the-run”) long-term bonds, the Treasury removes overall duration from the market. To fund these purchases, the Treasury issues short-term bills. This shifts supply to parts of the yield curve better equipped to absorb it. Critics argue that the sudden, unscheduled policy shift disrupts the Treasury’s traditional framework of being regular and predictable, causing further investor anxiety.

Bessent’s action is like putting a Band-Aid on a wound that needs a torniquet. He has joined Trump in an alternate reality. The market isn’t buying it.

When the government borrows hundreds of billions each month, it competes directly with private borrowers for capital. The massive government demand can push up overall interest rates across the entire economy. This means Americans end up paying significantly more for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and business loans.

And just like a household credit card, a larger balance means a larger monthly minimum payment. Net interest payments are quickly becoming one of the largest single components of the federal budget. Every dollar spent on interest is a dollar that cannot be spent on infrastructure, national defense, scientific research, tax cuts, or programs like Social Security and Medicare.

If investors eventually begin to worry that the U.S. will never be able to pay back its debt through normal revenues (taxes), they may fear that the government will simply print more money to cover the gap. Flooding the global economy with dollars to inflate away the debt devalues the currency. For us everyday Americans, this manifests as persistent, long-term inflation, reducing the purchasing power of our hard-earned savings and wages.

Time for Donnie and Bessent to play another round of golf.

ANALYSIS | Can Economic Anger Cost Republicans the Midterms?

WASHINGTON, D.C. / CIVICOHUB — August 17, 2026

Three months before Americans vote in the midterm elections, a political weakness is emerging for Republicans in perhaps the worst possible place:

the economy.

Donald Trump returned to the White House after making affordability one of the central arguments of his 2024 campaign. High grocery bills, gasoline prices and the broader cost of living had damaged Democrats badly.

Now the political equation is beginning to reverse.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed in early August found 37% of registered voters saying Democrats have the better approach to the economy, against 36% for Republicans. The difference is statistically tiny — effectively a tie — but historically significant: Republicans had enjoyed the advantage on this issue for most of the past decade.

The same poll put Democrats ahead 42% to 37% on the generic congressional ballot, with independents leaning Democratic by 12 points. Again, that national number cannot simply be translated into House seats. But with Republicans defending an exceptionally narrow majority, it is an unmistakable warning signal.

The question is no longer whether the economy will matter in November.

It is whether economic frustration becomes powerful enough to turn a difficult midterm environment into a loss of congressional power.

THE ECONOMY IS NOT COLLAPSING

The first thing an honest analysis must establish is that the United States is not in an economic collapse.

Real GDP grew at an annualized 1.5% in the second quarter, down from 2.1% in Q1 but still positive. Consumer spending, investment and exports all contributed to growth.

The problem for Republicans is that elections are rarely decided by whether GDP technically has a plus or minus sign in front of it.

They are decided by how people experience the economy.

July inflation remained 3.4% year over year. Energy costs have risen especially sharply, while the Iran conflict has pushed gasoline prices higher and placed renewed pressure on household budgets.

Food prices create the same political problem.

Reuters revisited Trump’s famous August 2024 grocery-table campaign event this weekend and calculated that the 26 grocery categories displayed there have risen another 3.4% during the first 19 months of his second term. That increase is far smaller than the inflation shock earlier in the decade, but it directly conflicts with the expectation among many voters that prices themselves would come back down.

That distinction matters:

Lower inflation does not mean lower prices.

It means prices are increasing more slowly.

For economists, that distinction is elementary.

For someone standing at a supermarket checkout, it can feel irrelevant.

THE MOST DANGEROUS NUMBER MAY BE CONSUMER CONFIDENCE

The University of Michigan’s preliminary August survey shows consumer sentiment falling roughly 8% in a single month, ending two months of improvement. Expectations for future business conditions deteriorated even more sharply.

But one detail is particularly important politically.

The largest August decline occurred among Republicans.

Republican consumer sentiment is now 19% below where it stood immediately before the Iran conflict and at its lowest level since the 2024 election.

That should worry GOP strategists more than Democratic anger.

A Democrat dissatisfied with Trump was probably already voting Democratic.

A Trump voter who believed his presidency would make daily life cheaper creates a different risk. That voter does not even need to become a Democrat.

They can become less enthusiastic.

They can skip a congressional race.

They can stay home.

In a House election decided by a few thousand votes, enthusiasm can matter almost as much as persuasion.

REPUBLICANS ARE LOSING THE ARGUMENT THAT HELPED THEM WIN

This may be the larger political story.

Republicans do not need voters to love the economy.

They need voters to believe Republicans are more capable of fixing it than Democrats.

That advantage is disappearing.

Reuters/Ipsos now essentially shows the two parties tied on economic stewardship, while cost of living remains one of the dominant issues voters say will influence their congressional vote.

This creates a political asymmetry for Trump.

He attacked the Biden administration relentlessly over prices and told voters he could bring them down.

That was effective because Americans already disliked what they were paying.

But once you make affordability a central promise, you also assume ownership of the issue after taking power.

Trump therefore does not necessarily need a recession to damage Republican candidates.

He simply needs enough voters to conclude:

“You promised my life would become more affordable. It hasn’t.”

Reuters found exactly that sentiment among some voters in competitive New Jersey, including people who supported Trump in 2024 but now say the cost of groceries remains a major frustration.

WHY THE HOUSE IS PARTICULARLY EXPOSED

Republicans currently hold 218 House seats, compared with 212 Democrats, one Independent and four vacancies.

That is not much of a cushion.

Cook Political Report currently classifies 19 House races as Toss-Ups, with additional seats sitting in Lean or Likely categories where a sufficiently strong national environment could make them competitive.

There is also the historical structure of midterms.

The president’s party usually faces an enthusiasm disadvantage because opposition voters have a powerful reason to turn out while some voters who elected the president two years earlier become disappointed, complacent or fatigued.

Trump adds another complication.

Pew found 42% of registered voters describe their 2026 congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 22% who see it as a vote for him.

Combine that with a five-point Democratic generic-ballot lead and a weakening Republican economic advantage, and the House becomes genuinely vulnerable.

None of this means Democrats are guaranteed control.

District boundaries matter. Candidate quality matters. Turnout matters. Only a relatively small share of 435 districts will determine the majority, and national polling cannot tell us precisely what will happen inside each one.

But Republicans do not have the luxury of needing a national collapse before they lose power.

Their majority is small enough that a modest anti-GOP movement could do it.

THE SENATE IS A DIFFERENT EQUATION

This is where predictions about a Democratic “wave” become too simplistic.

Republicans currently control the Senate 53–45, with two Independents.

Cook currently has four Senate contests rated Toss-Up, but Senate control depends on individual state races rather than the national popular mood alone.

That gives Republicans significantly more protection.

A national environment bad enough to flip several suburban House districts does not automatically create enough Democratic Senate victories.

Economic dissatisfaction can certainly make Republican Senate candidates' jobs harder.

But Democrats still need the right states, the right candidates and enough simultaneous victories.

That makes the most plausible split outcome under current conditions:

Democrats take the House while Republicans retain the Senate.

Not a prediction.

A scenario increasingly consistent with the present map.

THE IRAN WAR HAS BECOME AN ECONOMIC ISSUE TOO

Foreign policy and domestic economics are also becoming difficult to separate.

The Iran conflict has helped push fuel prices sharply higher. Reuters/Ipsos found that this energy shock is contributing to dissatisfaction with Trump’s economic management.

That creates an unusual feedback loop.

Trump argues the military campaign is necessary for national security.

But voters experience part of that strategy through the gasoline pump.

The president can ask Americans to accept those costs.

He cannot prevent them from factoring those costs into their vote.

That is especially dangerous because gasoline is one of the most visible prices in American life: voters see it displayed in giant numbers every time they drive past a station.

THREE MONTHS IS STILL A LONG TIME

There is one reason Republicans should not panic yet:

November 3 is not tomorrow.

Several things could materially change the political environment.

A sustained fall in gasoline prices could improve perceptions of affordability.

Stronger hiring could restore confidence.

Lower inflation could begin translating into improved real household income.

A foreign-policy breakthrough could reduce energy-market pressure.

Democrats could nominate weak candidates in critical districts.

Or some entirely different political issue could displace the economy.

The reverse is also true.

If hiring weakens further, prices remain elevated or consumer confidence continues falling, Republicans could enter October defending both their governing record and the economic issue that helped put Trump back in office.

That is a much more dangerous position.

CIVICOHUB ANALYSIS

As of August 17, the evidence does not support saying that economic dissatisfaction will cost Republicans the midterms.

It does support a stronger conclusion than merely saying Republicans have “a problem.”

The House majority is genuinely endangered, and economic dissatisfaction is becoming one of the clearest mechanisms through which Republicans could lose it.

The Senate remains more structurally favorable to the GOP.

The bigger strategic warning, however, goes beyond either chamber.

Republicans are losing their ownership of the economic argument.

For almost a decade, when American voters were unhappy about the economy, that usually benefited the GOP.

Now Americans remain unhappy — but they are no longer clearly convinced Republicans have the better answer.

That is a fundamental change.

And it leaves the midterms hanging on a deceptively simple question:

Will Americans feel materially better by November than they do today?

If the answer becomes yes, Republicans have time to recover.

If the answer remains no, Democrats may not need voters to embrace their economic program.

They may only need voters to punish the party already in power.

That is how economic dissatisfaction becomes an electoral wave.

Not massively impressed with Burnham's plan to scrap VAT on electricity bills.

Yes, it will help people struggling with their bills to some extent. But not by much.

And yes, it's a simple measure that's easy for the government to do quickly, so I suppose it has that in its favour.

And it's probably slightly progressive, in that people on minimum wage spend a greater proportion of their income on electricity than millionaires do.

But it's not massively progressive. Millionaires still spend a lot more on electricity than people on minimum wage, so they'll still benefit more in absolute terms.

If Burnham wants to help people struggling to pay their bills, raising the income tax threshold or the rates of Universal Credit would probably be better targeted.

Also, it encourages more energy use, which is not what we should be doing when the planet is burning.

SWANSEA: Nearly £700,000 for holiday food, activities and older residents — as summer fund jumps from last year’s £400k

More than 300 community groups across Swansea will share almost £700,000 to keep families fed and children busy through the school summer holidays.

The funding, part of Swansea Council‘s #Hereforyouthissummer campaign, covers food, activities and support with a focus on children, families and older people — and is up sharply from the £400,000 handed out last summer.

A total of 67 projects will provide food for school-aged children over the summer — which the council says will make sure families can still get help when free school meals are not available.

A further 56 emergency food providers will receive support to continue their work in communities across the county.

Keeping children active is the biggest slice of the fund: 120 successful bids that the council says will deliver free or low-cost activities for young people, from sports and creative sessions to community-based programmes.

Older residents are also a focus, the council said, with 64 funded projects offering activities for people aged 50 and over to stay active, reduce isolation and connect with others.

Among the groups receiving funding is the Bonymaen Kids Play Initiative, which runs activities after school and throughout the summer holidays.

Sarah Glover, who runs the group, said the money was important to its work: “We receive the school holiday food funding as well as play funding for activities.”

Council leader Rob Stewart said the school holidays could be “a challenging time for many families, particularly with the rising cost of living”.

“That’s why we’re working with hundreds of local groups to make sure children have access to food, fun activities and safe, welcoming spaces,” he said — adding it was also important to support older residents and the organisations “helping to tackle loneliness and build stronger neighbourhoods”.

Cllr Rebecca Fogarty, the council’s cabinet member for community support, said the funding would back “an incredible range of grassroots organisations that know their communities best and deliver services people can trust”.

“The #Hereforyouthissummer campaign is all about making sure no one feels left behind,” she added.

The council says the campaign brings together the range of support available to residents over the holidays — food provision, activities and community services — with details available from the authority.

It adds to a summer of help for family budgets: a new postcode website now lists where the Government’s summer VAT cut means cheaper days out and children’s meals.

SUMMER SAVINGS: Cheaper days out and kids’ meals at the click of a button — with Dan-yr-Ogof among the attractions signed up

Families across Swansea Bay can now type in their postcode and see where cheaper days out and children’s meals are on offer this summer — with one of the Swansea Valley’s best-known attractions among those signed up.

The UK Government’s Great British Summer Savings website has gone live, listing restaurants, cinemas and attractions that have pledged to pass on the Chancellor’s summer tax cut to customers.

VAT on a range of family activities was cut from 20% to 5% on 25 June, running until 1 September — covering family cinema tickets, admission to attractions for both children and adults, and children’s meals in restaurants.

Among those signed up is Dan-yr-Ogof, the showcaves centre in the upper Swansea Valley, alongside chains including Nando’s, Bill’s, Las Iguanas and ODEON — with Techniquest and Rhondda Heritage Park also on the list within day-trip range.

Using the site is simple: enter a postcode, set how far you’re willing to travel, and optionally filter by the type of attraction or food offer you’re after — and a list of participating businesses appears alongside a map.

There’s nothing to claim and no voucher codes: book a table or buy a ticket as normal, and the discount comes off the price automatically.

More than 1,700 businesses’ offers across the UK are on the site so far, and the government says it is speaking daily to businesses yet to join, to encourage them to sign up.

One point worth knowing: the tax cut itself applies to eligible sales everywhere, but it is up to each business whether to pass the saving on to customers — the website lists those that have committed to doing so.

The eligible activities cover children’s menu meals eaten in restaurants; children’s and family tickets for cinemas, theatres, concerts, shows and exhibitions; and admission for children and adults to attractions including amusement parks, fairs, museums, zoos, soft play centres, circuses, adventure parks, nature reserves and wildlife parks.

Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the tax cuts meant families would be able to enjoy “more of the little treats and days out that make the British summer holidays so special”.

“Our new website will make it easier for them to take advantage of Great British Summer Savings and help afford the moments that matter,” she said.

Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens said the UK Government was “helping families across Wales with the cost of living and putting more money back in their pockets”.

She said the VAT cut sat alongside action on fuel prices, increases to the National Minimum and Living Wage, and moves to cut energy bills.

The scheme runs until 1 September, with offers searchable at summersavings.gov.uk.

Step 1 — The Scam

Your 401(k) probably went up last year. You probably also felt like you were falling behind. Both things are true, and they’re connected in a way almost nobody talks about.

Here’s the contradiction: the stock market just had its best three-year run in a generation. And yet, most people’s actual lives — rent, groceries, childcare, a car that doesn’t break down — got harder, not easier. The market is booming. You’re not. Your grocery bill climbed. Your rent climbed. Your raise didn’t keep up. And somehow the people at the top of those ten companies became richer than some nations.

If that feels disconnected, it’s because the connection is hidden. The boom in the index isn’t your boom. It’s a boom for the owners of the ten companies, and you own a rounding error of them through your fund. The gains flow up; the costs flow down. That’s the entire machine in one sentence.

Why? Because you don’t own the market. You own a sliver of it. And that sliver has been quietly reshaped so that it’s no longer a bet on the broad economy — it’s a bet on one single thing.

Over the past three years, roughly 80% of the entire gain in the US stock market came from artificial intelligence. Not from factories hiring. Not from wages rising. Not from small businesses expanding. From AI.

And the ten largest companies in the S&P 500 — nearly all of them riding that AI wave — now make up more than 40% of the entire index. In 2000, at the peak of the dot-com bubble, tech was about 6% of the index. Today, AI-related stocks are over 30% by some measures.

So when your index fund goes up, it’s not because America got more productive. It’s because ten companies got more valuable. And when those ten stumble, your retirement goes with them.

The cruel part is that you didn’t choose this basket. Someone else built it, sold it to your fund manager as “diversified,” and now your retirement rides on whether those ten can outrun their own debt. You’re not an investor in AI. You’re collateral for it. And collateral doesn’t get a vote when the loan comes due.

This isn’t a normal sector doing well. This is concentration — and concentration is fragility. When all the eggs are in one basket, a crack in that basket shatters the whole tray. And right now, your eggs, your pension’s eggs, and your insurance company’s eggs are all in the AI basket.

Concentration like this has a history, and it never ends quietly. When a few firms dominate, they stop competing and start coordinating. Prices rise, wages stall, and risk piles up where nobody’s looking. The 2008 crisis wasn’t caused by one bad bank — it was caused by every bank holding the same bet. Today every major institution is holding the AI bet, and the bet is bigger.

Step 2 — The Mechanism

So who’s actually behind this, and what’s keeping it propped up? Follow the money, and you find debt — historic, record-breaking debt.

Start with the cost side. To build frontier AI you need data centers, chip clusters, and power — enormous amounts of all three. In 2025 alone, AI-related corporate debt issuance exceeded $200 billion. Oracle issued $18 billion in bonds in a single month. Meta issued $30 billion — the largest corporate bond deal since 2023. Goldman Sachs called 2025 a “banner year” for AI bonds, with more coming in 2026. None of that borrowing is free; every dollar has to be repaid, with interest, from revenue that hasn’t arrived yet.

This debt isn’t backed by healthy cash flows. Oracle is now spending 57% of its revenue on AI infrastructure. Microsoft is at 45%. Across the biggest players, AI infrastructure is eating close to 94% of the cash their core businesses throw off. There is no cushion left. If a single project misses, there’s nothing to absorb the hit. Imagine a household where 94% of every paycheck goes to one loan — that’s the position these companies are in, except their “paycheck” is the cloud business you and every other company already pay for.

And the financing is circular in a way that should worry you. Nvidia agreed to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI — but much of that money flows right back to Nvidia as OpenAI buys chips. The investment firm GMO compared this to the circular financing of the dot-com era, the exact thing that made so many companies fragile back then. Michael Burry warned that depreciation schedules for data-center chips — booked at 5 to 6 years instead of a realistic 2 to 3 — could be hiding more than $175 billion in losses already sustained. In plain terms: they’re pretending the hardware lasts twice as long as it does, so the books look better than reality.

Now look at the revenue side, because that’s where the whole structure leans. Sequoia Capital estimated the AI industry needs to generate about $600 billion in new annual revenue just to justify what’s already been spent. By 2025 that gap widened to roughly $800 billion. Annual AI infrastructure spending is about $650 billion. Actual revenue is about $50 billion. That’s a $600 billion hole, every single year.

To make that concrete: imagine a restaurant that spent $650,000 on a kitchen and serves $50,000 of food. Then it borrows another $200,000 to build a bigger kitchen, confident the customers will show up. That’s the AI industry, except the “restaurant” is the backbone of your pension. The bet is that demand will explode before the loans come due. So far, it hasn’t.

The three biggest cloud providers spent over $150 billion in capex in 2024, yet AI-related revenue is less than 5% of their total. And MIT studied how generative AI actually performs inside companies and found that 95% of corporate AI projects produced no measurable impact on profits. Not small returns — zero. For a young industry with the most expensive infrastructure buildout in human history, that’s not a speed bump. That’s existential.

Consider what that means in plain terms. A bank deploys an AI chatbot that answers customer questions. It costs millions to build and run. The MIT study says it didn’t move the profit needle. But the bank still has to pay for the chips, the data center, and the power — and that cost lands in the same place your fees and your interest rate come from. The AI didn’t make the bank more efficient. It made the bank more expensive to run, and you’re the one covering the difference.

Now the macro tightens around all of it. The Fed is signaling possible rate hikes, not cuts, because inflation won’t die. Japan’s central bank just raised rates to a 31-year high, pulling global liquidity back — the exact liquidity that high-risk bets like AI depend on. Higher rates make every dollar of that infrastructure debt more expensive to carry, and they punish the “profit-later” models of OpenAI and Anthropic most harshly. The money that was free is now expensive, and the bills are due.

The timing couldn’t be worse for the borrowers. They built the debt when money was nearly free. Now that money costs real interest, and the revenue to pay it still hasn’t shown up. A household that bought a house with a teaser-rate mortgage faces the same wall: the cheap period ends, the payment jumps, and the income never rose to match.

But here’s the part almost nobody covers: a geopolitical rival found a way to make all of this much worse.

In January 2025, a Chinese company called DeepSeek released a model that performed nearly as well as America’s best — at a fraction of the cost. Within days, about one trillion dollars in US AI market value evaporated. Nvidia set the record for the largest single-day loss by any company in history.

How did they do it? Largely through distillation — training a smaller, cheaper model on the outputs of a larger one. In February 2025, Anthropic accused three Chinese labs of running over 16 million queries through roughly 24,000 fake accounts to distill its Claude model. In April, the White House accused China of “industrial-scale campaigns to steal American AI models.” In June, Anthropic told the Senate that Alibaba ran the largest such effort yet — 28.8 million interactions through 25,000 fake accounts.

Think of it like a student who photocopies the honor student’s notes, then sells a cheaper study guide. The notes were expensive to produce; the copy is cheap. Distillation itself is legal. Every major lab does it to its own models. The problem is when a rival nation does it to a competitor’s model, then deploys the cheap result to undercut the revenue base of the industry it’s targeting.

The price gap is enormous. Chinese open-source models cost about five times less to use than top US models, while scoring within a few points on standard benchmarks. Coinbase cut its AI bill nearly in half by shifting to Chinese open-source models. Lindy, a US AI company, moved off Claude onto DeepSeek when its AI costs grew larger than its payroll. An estimated 80% of US AI startups now use Chinese open-source models.

This isn’t a price war. It’s a strategy to weaken the revenue stream American AI companies desperately need to service their debt. When a competitor offers a product that’s 80% as good for 20% of the price, the market leader can’t raise prices — and may have to lower them. That’s exactly what China wants. It doesn’t need its own AI firms to be profitable short-term; state support can sustain losses indefinitely, as long as the strategic goal — undermining US profitability — is achieved.

Compare it to how a discount retailer undercuts a local shop: the newcomer doesn’t need to win on margin, just on volume and patience. China can fund its labs through state banks that answer to industrial policy, not quarterly earnings. The US firms answer to shareholders who want growth now. That asymmetry is the whole game. One side can lose money for a decade; the other can’t survive two bad quarters.

And the damage isn’t only to stock prices. AI infrastructure needs power — staggering amounts of it. Data centers are now competing with households for electricity in parts of the country, and that competition shows up in your utility bill. The same debt that’s propping up the AI bet is also bidding up the cost of keeping your lights on. You’re paying for the boom twice: once through your index fund, once through your meter.

The people whose pensions are being loaded with AI debt didn’t vote for that exposure. The boom is concentrated at the top; the bill is spread across everyone. That’s the defining feature of this moment — not that AI exists, but that the upside accrues to a handful of owners while the downside risk is socialized to the public.

And the risk is being spread to you. Banks making these loans know how shaky this is, so they’re doing what they did in 2008: slicing up the risky debt, dressing it as safe, and selling it off. A law firm tracking this found lenders pooling AI data-center loans and selling pieces to pension funds, insurers, and asset managers. The Federal Reserve reported major life insurers already have nearly a trillion dollars tied up in private debt. Pension funds have started committing to debt funds fueling Meta and Oracle.

That means the risk isn’t contained in Silicon Valley. It’s in your pension, your insurance, your “safe” bond fund — and, as we opened, your index fund. If the AI bubble bursts, the losses land on teachers’ pensions and union retirement plans, not just hedge funds. And here’s the trap: by spreading the risk so wide, the banks create a political imperative. If AI stumbles, the government feels forced to bail it out, because the damage would otherwise be too broad. That’s the “too big to fail” playbook, reprised for the AI era.

We’ve seen this movie. In 2008, the banks bundled mortgage debt, sold it as safe, and when it cracked, the public paid. The executives kept their bonuses; the taxpayers ate the loss. The AI version uses data-center loans instead of mortgages, but the structure is identical: private gain, public risk. The only difference is the scale — and this time the bet is bigger than the entire 2008 housing market was at its peak.

Step 3 — The Subliminal Step

Step back from the names and the numbers. Look at the structure.

This isn’t a few bad actors scheming. The incentive structure rewards exactly this behavior. When the goal is infinite growth on a finite planet, and when executives are paid in stock that peaks this quarter, the rational move is to borrow now, build now, and let the future sort out the bill. The shareholder-first model doesn’t care whether the revenue arrives. It can’t — its job is the next earnings call, not the next decade.

And once the debt is big enough and spread widely enough, failure becomes unthinkable — not because the business is sound, but because the damage from failure would be too broad. That’s the leverage the borrowers hold over everyone else. They don’t need to succeed. They need to be too big to fail.

The AI companies already know this. Notice the order of operations. Build the debt first. Make it systemic second. Ask for the bailout third. By the time the request arrives, the alternative — a crater in every pension and insurer that holds the paper — is worse than paying up. That’s not corruption in the cartoon sense. It’s the system working exactly as designed, with the public positioned to absorb the loss. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s CEO calls for binding regulation and the power to block any model deemed dangerous. On the surface that’s safety. But the same rules that make AI “safer” also raise barriers to entry — making it harder for open-source competitors, especially small ones, to exist. The government is caught between its stated commitment to free markets and its strategic need to maintain AI supremacy. You can’t avoid this bet. Your pension, your insurance, your index fund — they’re already tied to AI. You don’t need to invest in AI. AI already invested in you.

That’s the whole game at the local level — not a revolution, just a question asked loud enough that the people managing your money have to answer it.

Support the boring, unglamorous rules that actually shift leverage. Utility board elections decide who gets priority on the grid — and right now, data centers are winning that fight in some states. AI will change the world. That’s almost certain. But the current constellation of companies, debts, and investors may not survive to see that world. The people who built the data centers, trained the models, and paid the electric bills will still be here. The question is whether they own any of the upside — or whether they were just the ones holding the basket when it dropped.

So read the next earnings headline with this in mind: every record high in the index is a record high in your exposure to one bet. That doesn’t mean sell everything. This isn’t a price war. It’s a strategy to weaken the revenue stream American AI companies desperately need to service their debt. When a competitor offers a product that’s 80% as good for 20% of the price, the market leader can’t raise prices — and may have to lower them. That’s exactly what China wants. It doesn’t need its own AI firms to be profitable short-term; state support can sustain losses indefinitely, as long as the strategic goal — undermining US profitability — is achieved.

Compare it to how a discount retailer undercuts a local shop: the newcomer doesn’t need to win on margin, just on volume and patience. China can fund its labs through state banks that answer to industrial policy, not quarterly earnings. The US firms answer to shareholders who want growth now. That asymmetry is the whole game. One side can lose money for a decade; the other can’t survive two bad quarters.

And the damage isn’t only to stock prices. AI infrastructure needs power — staggering amounts of it. Data centers are now competing with households for electricity in parts of the country, and that competition shows up in your utility bill. The same debt that’s propping up the AI bet is also bidding up the cost of keeping your lights on. You’re paying for the boom twice: once through your index fund, once through your meter.

Think about who’s actually carrying this. The people who built the data centers aren’t sharing in the stock gains — they’re paid by the hour, and their raises haven’t outpaced the rent. The people whose pensions are being loaded with AI debt didn’t vote for that exposure. The boom is concentrated at the top; the bill is spread across everyone. That’s the defining feature of this moment — not that AI exists, but that the upside accrues to a handful of owners while the downside risk is socialized to the public.

And the risk is being spread to you. Banks making these loans know how shaky this is, so they’re doing what they did in 2008: slicing up the risky debt, dressing it as safe, and selling it off. A law firm tracking this found lenders pooling AI data-center loans and selling pieces to pension funds, insurers, and asset managers. The Federal Reserve reported major life insurers already have nearly a trillion dollars tied up in private debt. Pension funds have started committing to debt funds fueling Meta and Oracle.

That means the risk isn’t contained in Silicon Valley. It’s in your pension, your insurance, your “safe” bond fund — and, as we opened, your index fund. If the AI bubble bursts, the losses land on teachers’ pensions and union retirement plans, not just hedge funds. And here’s the trap: by spreading the risk so wide, the banks create a political imperative. If AI stumbles, the government feels forced to bail it out, because the damage would otherwise be too broad. That’s the “too big to fail” playbook, reprised for the AI era.

We’ve seen this movie. In 2008, the banks bundled mortgage debt, sold it as safe, and when it cracked, the public paid. The executives kept their bonuses; the taxpayers ate the loss. The AI version uses data-center loans instead of mortgages, but the structure is identical: private gain, public risk. The only difference is the scale — and this time the bet is bigger than the entire 2008 housing market was at its peak.

Step 3 — The Subliminal Step

Step back from the names and the numbers. Look at the structure.

This isn’t a few bad actors scheming. The incentive structure rewards exactly this behavior. When the goal is infinite growth on a finite planet, and when executives are paid in stock that peaks this quarter, the rational move is to borrow now, build now, and let the future sort out the bill. The shareholder-first model doesn’t care whether the revenue arrives. It can’t — its job is the next earnings call, not the next decade.

And once the debt is big enough and spread widely enough, failure becomes unthinkable — not because the business is sound, but because the damage from failure would be too broad. That’s the leverage the borrowers hold over everyone else. They don’t need to succeed. They need to be too big to fail.

The AI companies already know this. In November 2024, OpenAI floated the idea that the federal government should backstop its financing — that taxpayers should help guarantee the debt behind its buildout. The backlash was immediate, and the company walked it back. But the CEO had previously said that “when something gets big enough, the government is the insurer of last resort.”

Notice the order of operations. Build the debt first. Make it systemic second. Ask for the bailout third. By the time the request arrives, the alternative — a crater in every pension and insurer that holds the paper — is worse than paying up. That’s not corruption in the cartoon sense. It’s the system working exactly as designed, with the public positioned to absorb the loss. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s CEO calls for binding regulation and the power to block any model deemed dangerous. On the surface that’s safety. But the same rules that make AI “safer” also raise barriers to entry — making it harder for open-source competitors, especially small ones, to exist. And the hardest competitors to regulate are exactly the cheap open-source models flowing out of China. So the push for regulation, sold as public protection, conveniently serves to protect incumbent US companies from foreign competition — while building the political case for future bailouts.

When you see the same firms asking for both a bailout and a moat, understand what’s happening: they want the public to carry the risk and the incumbents to keep the reward. That’s not a contradiction to them. It’s the strategy.

So the crack in the basket isn’t a bug. It’s what happens when an entire system bets everything on one unproven payoff while loading the risk onto everyone else. The technology may deliver. The companies holding the debt may not survive to see it.

Look at the government’s dilemma, because it tells you everything about who gets protected. The AI companies are already positioning for a bailout. In November 2024, OpenAI floated the idea that the federal government should backstop its financing — that taxpayers should help guarantee the debt behind its buildout. The backlash was immediate, and the company walked it back. But the CEO had previously said that “when something gets big enough, the government is the insurer of last resort.” That’s not a slip. That’s a request, stated plainly.

At the same time, Anthropic’s CEO calls for binding regulation, mandatory safety testing, and the power to block any model deemed dangerous. On the surface that’s about safety. But many analysts point out the same rules that make AI “safer” also raise barriers to entry — making it harder for open-source competitors, especially small startups, to exist at all. And the hardest competitors to regulate are exactly the cheap open-source models flowing out of China. So the push for regulation, sold as public protection, conveniently serves to protect incumbent US companies from foreign competition — while building the political case for future bailouts.

This is a classic pattern: when an industry can’t win on price, it tries to win on regulation. And when it can’t survive on its own, it demands state support. The government is caught between its stated commitment to free markets and its strategic need to maintain AI supremacy. But the market has already shown it can’t sustain itself without intervention — and the state, in turn, is reluctant to let the industry fail because AI now accounts for a huge slice of America’s economic growth.

Every major infrastructure revolution followed this arc. Canals in Britain, railways in Britain and the US, the internet — they all went on to change the world, but the first wave of investors was wiped out. The technology delivered on its promise; the revenue came too slowly to save those who borrowed too much, too soon. AI is different in one respect: the price pressure isn’t normal competition. It’s a geopolitical rival deliberately undercutting the industry’s ability to generate revenue. China doesn’t need its AI firms to be profitable. It only needs American AI firms to be unprofitable long enough for the debt to become unsustainable.

Step 4 — The Leverage

You can’t avoid this bet. Your pension, your insurance, your index fund — they’re already tied to AI. You don’t need to invest in AI. AI already invested in you.

But you can protect yourself by knowing what you actually own. Ask where your yield comes from. Look at the concentration in your index funds — if ten companies are 40% of your “diversified” portfolio, you’re not diversified. A target-date fund marketed as safe still rides the same basket. Diversify beyond AI, not because AI won’t succeed, but because the timing is uncertain and the debt overhang is real.

Push for transparency where you have a voice. If you have a pension or 401(k) with a fiduciary board, ask what exposure it has to private AI debt. Those boards answer to members, and pressure from members changes what they buy. You have a right to know if your retirement is backed by circular chip financing.

There are already examples of this working. Public pension members in several states have forced boards to disclose private-debt exposure and, in some cases, to cap it. None of that made headlines. It didn’t need to. A single board vote, prompted by a few members asking the right question, shifted where millions in retirement money goes. That’s the whole game at the local level — not a revolution, just a question asked loud enough that the people managing your money have to answer it.

Support the boring, unglamorous rules that actually shift leverage. Utility board elections decide who gets priority on the grid — and right now, data centers are winning that fight in some states. Show up to those meetings, or at least track who your pension is backing in those votes. Antitrust enforcement against the giants isn’t radical; it’s how markets are supposed to work when one basket holds everyone’s eggs.

And talk about this. The reason the risk stays hidden is that the language stays technical. When you say “my index fund is 40% ten companies,” people get it. When you say “my pension is holding AI data-center debt that’s been sliced and sold,” people get it. The system survives on everyone assuming someone else is watching. Nobody is.

Look at the pattern across your own life. The same logic — borrow big, concentrate, socialize the risk — shows up in your rent, your hospital bill, and your streaming subscription. Private equity buys the building, loads it with debt, and raises your rent. A private equity chain buys the hospital, and the quality drops while the bill climbs. Three companies own most of what you stream, and the price keeps rising while the content thins. Same model, different aisle.

Diversification isn’t just buying a different fund. It’s recognizing that the same concentrated bet is wired into everything you “own” indirectly. If your pension holds the debt, your insurer holds the debt, and your index fund holds the equity, you’re triple-exposed to one story. The practical move is to map those exposures and push each one toward something broader. You won’t win the argument by yourself — but a room of pension members asking the same question changes what the board buys.

The historical lesson is brutal: having the right thesis with the wrong timing is the same as being wrong. Every infrastructure revolution — canals, railways, the internet — changed the world, but the first wave of investors was wiped out. The technology delivered; the revenue came too slowly to save those who borrowed too much, too soon.

And the workers building this — the data-center technicians, the annotators labeling training data for poverty wages, the utility crews keeping the lights on — they’re not the ones with stock options. They’re the ones whose labor produces the value that flows to the top. When the boom is concentrated and the risk is socialized, the people doing the actual work are left holding nothing but the bill. That’s not a flaw in execution. It’s the design.

You can bet on the right technology and still get hammered by the debt and the concentration. The people wiped out in 2008 weren’t the ones who thought housing would never crash. They were the ones over-leveraged and over-concentrated when it did.

Your retirement shouldn’t rise and fall on whether ten companies can outrun their own debt. But it does — until enough of us notice the basket has all our eggs in it, and ask who decided that was a good idea, and who gets to walk away when it breaks.

The system isn’t mysterious. It’s a set of choices about who owns what, who bears the risk, and who collects the gain. Those choices got made in boardrooms and regulator offices, not in your name. The only counterweight is enough people deciding the arrangement is unacceptable — and acting on it where they actually have leverage: their pension votes, their utility board, their antitrust regulators, their own willingness to say the quiet part out loud.

AI will change the world. That’s almost certain. But the current constellation of companies, debts, and investors may not survive to see that world. The people who built the data centers, trained the models, and paid the electric bills will still be here. The question is whether they own any of the upside — or whether they were just the ones holding the basket when it dropped.

So read the next earnings headline with this in mind: every record high in the index is a record high in your exposure to one bet. That doesn’t mean sell everything. It means know the basket, name the risk, and stop pretending the boom at the top has anything to do with the life at the bottom. It doesn’t. And the people who built the machine are counting on you not noticing.

LLANELLI: Nearly 7,000 items handed to families in need as town charities join anti-poverty drive

Nearly 7,000 items of clothing and household goods have been handed to families in need in Llanelli, through a partnership between local charities and a Swansea-based “multibank.”

The drive has been spearheaded by Llanelli town councillor Shaun Greaney, who has been working to bring the Cwtch Mawr Multibank’s reach to the town and the wider county.

The Multibank takes surplus goods donated by major companies — items that might once have gone to landfill — and redistributes them, in pristine condition, to people who need them.

Councillor Greaney said nearly 7,000 clothing and household items had been issued to people in difficult circumstances.

The help was delivered in partnership with seven local organisations: Ty Gwyn Church, Tyisha Foodbank, Myrtle House Foodbank, Llanelli LLAMAS (the Llanelli Autistic Mothers Association), Llanelli Women’s Refuge, the Links mental health charity, and Morfa Family Centre.

A batch of free baby milk for infants aged up to 12 months has also been distributed, going to the Llanelli Foodbank at Myrtle House, Tyisha Foodbank and Llanelli LLAMAS.

Cllr Shaun Greaney delivering aid to Llanelli Women’s Refuge. Image: Cllr Shaun Greaney

Councillor Greaney, who represents the Lliedi ward, said he had seen poverty at close quarters.

“It is a scourge on our society,” he said. “It leads to premature deaths and blights the lives of too many families. I am determined to do everything I can to tackle this through direct action and hard work.”

He described the approach as “hugs not handouts,” saying it was about preserving people’s dignity.

“It delivers dignity. It allows families to function. It helps keep the wolf from the door,” he said.

He said one story in particular had stayed with him.

“I have heard of a young girl, aged nine, who received a pair of new shoes as a result of the Multibank’s work — she was thrilled and had tears in her eyes,” he said. “Because she had never had anything new in her life.”

He added that it was “heartbreaking” to hear that children were sometimes taken into care with their belongings in black bin bags.

“Hugs not handouts” at Links: manager Michele Rees, left, with Cllr Shaun Greaney and his wife Melanie. Image: Cllr Shaun Greaney

Councillor Greaney said councils and councillors of all parties should put tackling poverty at the top of the agenda, and was critical of the impact of what he called “fourteen years of Tory austerity” on public services.

He paid tribute to the charities and volunteers who had taken the project on, saying they had helped cut through red tape to reach the people who needed help most.

The Cwtch Mawr Multibank was the idea of former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown, and works with companies including Amazon to redistribute unsold goods.

Run in Swansea in partnership with the charity Faith in Families, it has given out almost 1.5 million items across the Swansea Bay area, with support from the Welsh Government and Swansea Council.

The Multibank has steadily expanded across the region, including a pilot into Neath Port Talbot and, more recently, into Bridgend.

Councillor Greaney said Carmarthenshire County Council had agreed to establish something similar in the county, but that this had not yet happened.

Wider hopes for the town

Councillor Greaney also welcomed the £20 million Pride in Place project for Llanelli, a 10-year regeneration scheme he said could “transform the prospects of our town and its people.”

He welcomed the appointment of Steve Donoghue as the project’s independent chairman, and said he hoped the board running it would be made up of people with a track record of making a difference. Residents are currently being invited to apply to sit on that board.

He praised Llanelli MP Dame Nia Griffith for securing the money, and said that used wisely — alongside Carmarthenshire County Council’s town centre projects — it could “deliver hope where there has been despair.”

CHEQUE MATE: Lloyds caves in and brings back Post Office cheque deposits after MP backlash

Lloyds has been forced into a U-turn over a banking service that thousands of customers rely on — after stripping it away earlier this year.

The bank had quietly become the only major UK lender to stop customers paying cheques into their accounts at the Post Office, scrapping the service across branches and Banking Hubs.

Now, after a backlash from MPs and campaigners, it has agreed to bring it back.

Lloyds says it has asked the Post Office to keep accepting cheque deposits into Lloyds accounts until the end of 2030 — though the climbdown still hinges on the two sides agreeing terms.

The reversal followed a letter signed by 121 MPs from every corner of the Commons, demanding Lloyds boss Charlie Nunn think again.

Among them was Ben Lake, the Plaid Cymru MP for Ceredigion Preseli, whose largely rural seat borders Carmarthenshire.

Campaigners warned the move had hit the people least able to cope with it — older customers, disabled people, and those locked out of online banking, along with the charities, clubs and small firms that still deal in cheques.

And it landed at the worst possible time for south-west Wales, where high street banks have been shutting their doors at a relentless pace.

Lloyds itself is part of that retreat, having confirmed it will close its branches in Ammanford and Gorseinon in 2026.

The Halifax in Llanelli — also part of Lloyds Banking Group — is due to close in November, while the TSB name is set to vanish from high streets altogether after Santander’s takeover.

As the branches disappear, more and more people have been left leaning on the Post Office and new Banking Hubs, like the one confirmed for Gorseinon, just to get to a counter.

For those customers, being able to pay in a cheque around the corner is not a nicety — it is a lifeline.

In its response to MPs, Lloyds said it had listened to feedback from customers and parliamentarians.

The bank said keeping the service going until 2030 would help make sure customers “who may need more time are supported,” adding that for some — particularly older and vulnerable people — “familiarity and reassurance remain important.”

Mr Lake welcomed the move but warned Lloyds not to leave the job half done.

“I welcome Lloyds’ decision to seek the restoration of cheque deposit services at Post Office branches,” he said.

“Access to local Post Offices is essential for people across Ceredigion Preseli, as it keeps face-to-face banking available for residents, small businesses and community groups.”

He said it was “a matter of fairness” that people who rely on cheques — “often elderly, vulnerable or digitally excluded” — should not be forced to wrestle with apps, post their cheques, or travel miles when rival banks already allowed deposits at the Post Office.

He said that while Lloyds had “moved in the right direction,” it now needed “a concrete agreement” so its customers got the same access other banks already offered.

The campaign drew backing from right across the political divide, including the Conservatives’ Mel Stride, the Liberal Democrats’ Daisy Cooper, Green MP Adrian Ramsay and Jeremy Corbyn, now leader of Your Party.

While Post Office customers have still been able to take out and pay in cash, scrapping cheque deposits had left some with no easy way to bank their money close to home.

SWANSEA: Cheaper days out and meals as summer VAT cut takes effect — here’s what’s included

Families in Swansea face cheaper days out this summer, after a temporary cut to VAT on children’s meals, cinema tickets and family attractions came into force this week.

The reduction is part of a UK Government scheme, branded “Great British Summer Savings,” running from 25 June until 1 September.

It cuts the VAT rate on a range of family activities from 20% to 5% across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The lower rate applies to children’s menu meals eaten in restaurants, and to children’s and family tickets for cinemas, theatres, concerts, shows and exhibitions.

It also covers admission to attractions including theme parks, soft play centres, museums, zoos, fairs, adventure parks, nature reserves and wildlife parks.

In Swansea, that means cheaper visits to local restaurants, pubs and family attractions — from independents such as the Secret Bar and Kitchen to chains like Nando’s.

The scheme follows the VAT cut first announced in May, which will run through the school summer holidays.

Swansea West MP Torsten Bell, a Treasury minister who helped put the discounts in place, welcomed the move.

“Families across Swansea will be able to enjoy their summer holidays that bit more this year,” he said.

He said he was “delighted at the boost this will give to the many fantastic local pubs, restaurants and attractions.”

Bell said the focus on living standards was “exactly right,” and that the scheme would help bring down bills.

The government has said it expects businesses to pass the VAT savings on to customers — though there is no requirement for them to do so, meaning the size of any discount at the till will vary from place to place.

The cut comes on top of other cost-of-living measures, including a £150 reduction in energy bills and a freeze on fuel duty.

For families weighing up how to fill the six-week break, the savings could take the edge off the cost of eating out and visiting attractions across the city and beyond.

Parents are being encouraged to check with individual venues to see how the reduced rate is being applied before booking.
